draft.title: Yield and purity
card: the actual mass of product made, divided by the theoretical (greatest possible) mass, then × 100. The theoretical mass is worked out from the balanced equation and the limiting reagent.
the share of a sample that is the wanted substance. Purity (%) = mass of wanted substance ÷ mass of sample × 100.
Yield and purity are separate measures. A high yield can still be impure, if the mass collected includes by-products or leftover reactants.
Yield can be lost through incomplete reactions, side reactions and product left behind during separation. Purification, such as recrystallisation, can raise purity but usually lowers yield.
draft.remember: Yield asks how much was made compared with the most possible. Purity asks how much of the sample is the wanted substance.

a.q: A student collects 4.2 g of a product. The balanced equation shows the most that could form is 6.0 g. What is the percentage yield?
a.why: Percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100 = 4.2 ÷ 6.0 × 100 = 70%. Turning the fraction upside down gives 143%, but a yield here cannot be above 100% when the product is pure and the theoretical mass is the most possible.
a.clue: Actual mass goes on top, theoretical mass goes below.

b.q: Dev makes 9.0 g of crystals. Tests show only 7.2 g of the crystals is the wanted compound. What is the purity of the sample?
b.why: Purity = wanted substance ÷ mass of sample × 100 = 7.2 ÷ 9.0 × 100 = 80%. The 72% option is tempting, but it just uses the digits of 7.2 and ignores the sample mass.
b.clue: Compare the wanted substance with the whole sample, not with a theoretical mass.
